comments.author: scriptsmith
comments.text:
From the security page [0]
> Don’t use the emulator to test the following:
> - IAM policies and permissions boundaries
> - Resource-based policies, such as bucket policies
> - AWS KMS key policies
> - Access across AWS accounts or across AWS Regions
> - Any other security control
> Some services in the emulator evaluate IAM policies for IAM users and roles that you create in the emulator, but not the same way as AWS. The emulator never denies a request signed with its own key. It doesn’t check AWS KMS key policies or Amazon S3 bucket policies. It also doesn’t support calls across accounts or Regions. So a request that AWS denies might succeed in the emulator. A request that AWS allows might fail.
This is a shame because I'd love for the official AWS product to be better than e.g. ministack and localstack on this, which will go some of the distance. I think because the agents were only building on the public API surface, it's hard to build this part. But they should've tried and let the agents read whatever policy engines AWS has. Or maybe it's a way to prevent someone from trivially running aws-emulator as AWSaaS?

stories.title_en: Lock Your GitHub Actions

comments.author: woodruffw
comments.text:
The advice here is really great (as I'd expect from Hugo), but as the maintainer of zizmor I want to note some caveats with the current iteration of workflow lockfiles:
- They only lock normal action calls. If your workflows invoke other reusable workflows, you need to keep those hash-pinned manually for now.
- Composite actions are not
themselves
locked. Instead, they get locked transitively through their callsites i.e. the workflows that call them. This makes any individual caller that uses lockfiles safe, but it also makes the current `gh actions-lock` default
unsafe
(since it removes hash-pins from the composite action itself, meaning that any external caller that invokes the action loses their transitive pinning).
- Other forms of `uses:` clauses, like Docker images, are also not currently locked via the lockfile. And the same for forms of interior mutability (like an action running `npx ...` under the hood, although the latter is fully outside of GitHub's control to prevent. But these mean that you
can't
assume that a fully locked Actions setup is in fact 100% immutable.
I hope they address these gaps soon, because it's otherwise an excellent (and long-awaited) feature.

comments.author: ryankrage77
comments.text:
I'm reminded of that adage "Given the opportunity, players will optimise the fun out of a game". A fully automated setup is cool, but if it's working well, there's not much to do. You're not gardening any more.
I have a bunch of plants on my window sill, and considered getting moisture sensors and automating watering, but I realised that kind of defeats the point of looking after the plants myself. On top of the satisfaction of manual work, I recently realised that it's taught me an intuition - the quirks of how much water each plant wants at different times of year (even cacti are thirsty in summer!), and how soil composition and pot size affects water retention. It's probably not generally transferable knowledge, but it was fun to realise I'd come to know my plants really well.

comments.author: TSiege
comments.text:
This story is very cool, and it’s exciting to see how much progress AI will bring to every field. One thing to temper everyone from wanting to lidar the whole world is human capacity. Finding discoveries like this is essentially as hard as doing the lidar mapping. Now the issue will be getting archaeologist there in time before someone else does.
The best way to protect a site is to leave it alone. If we start finding dozens or hundreds of sites it will be more than what archaeologists can excavate and protest. Treasure hunters and looters don’t care about stratigraphy and the processes involved for doing research. Maybe the cat is out of the bag on this one, but good for thought.
Edit: I’m not saying we shouldn’t have people use AI to do this or that no bad actor will. This comment is in response to the sentiment I am seeing in the comments that we should lidar the whole world and have AI find any anomalous structures it can. There is no way for archeologists to excavate and protect all those places in that scenario

comments.author: hanoz
comments.text:
I created the first online lidar map of the UK (well, England and Wales), as announced here many years ago! (now at
https://lidarmap.uk
) and delightfully there have been dozens of finds of previously unknown sites of archaeological significance found using it that I'm aware of. Roman villas, forts, henges, all sorts of earthworks. New discoveries are being reported using this and similar tools almost weekly, on forums like
https://www.reddit.com/r/LiDARdiscoveryUK/
. Britain really is littered with this stuff.
Although it does feel the finds are getting increasingly hard to spot, every now and then you get a
how did everyone miss that
moment. Perhaps not surprisingly, most of the remaining impressive finds tend to be in woodland, using the Digital Terrain Model data which can peer beneath the forest canopy, like this Mexican one today, or are within newly released coverage which is promptly pounced on by armchair archeologists.
Not sure what my point is here except... to me this story still feels like a function of the amazing recent progress in lidar coverage and data availability (not to mention the incredible technology behind it), rather than an AI one, although I don't doubt

comments.author: buryat
comments.text: It seems obvious that if replication of elementary particles appears that everything else will be an emerging property given enough time. And if you look at atoms and math there're definite parallels that once atoms can interconnect stronger than everything else (considering the 3d world) and something like Penrose's tiles where you get repeating interconnecting structures that more higher level structures would be possible. And with energy connected to the particles momentum and Heisenberg's uncertainty principle you get fluctuations in the structures that allow for both new structures and enforcing of the construction rules. You also have clear levels between forces that work on different levels that create boundaries to the structures. 3 spacial dimensions give additional directions of interactions between structures. And voila, given conditions, there's a place for emerging properties. Whether it was RNA who knows. It does seem that the search becomes way murkier toward going into the actual mechanism but the ingredients seem to be in place

comments.author: alphasm
comments.text:
Is there a reason why the alternative idea of closed autocatalytic sets from Stuart Kauffman doesn't get nearly as much attention or discussion as the RNA origin hypothesis?
Ever since I first learned about it, it seems to me a much more likely origin of life hypothesis, as it doesn't require something to catalyze itself, which causes inevitable problems with mutation causing loss of catalytic efficiency.
Also, it is not incompatible with RNA being one of the early building blocks. It just doesn't require RNA to be where everything started.

comments.author: MarceliusK
comments.text: I think the biggest unresolved question isn't whether RNA can replicate itself, but how you get from occasional replication to a self-sustaining system

comments.author: Neb_OoL
comments.text:
The hardest part of the transition from prebiotic chemistry (assembling the building blocks) to an 'RNA World' is doing so in a way that can support RNA copying. As others have shown the chance of finding one replicator is low - so you need supporting RNA copying chemistry at a pretty substantial level to help that happen.
This is where the hard part of the field is currently: finding chemistry that can support accurate RNA copying that is also both sufficiently high yielding and also compatible with these reactions being inside protocells (fatty acids for example). An RNA genome only really has value when it can be selfish and keep any innovations it makes to itself inside a protocell!
I work in Origins Research - if you have questions please ask and ill try to answer with the current opinions of the field!

stories.title_en: Faster Retrieval for Better, More Efficient RAG

comments.author: armcat
comments.text:
Just yesterday I saw a talk from Spotify where they presented their own fast retrieval mechanism "Parallel Fusion Router" [1]. It's also in the "learned retrieval" paradigm - in their case they use a teacher LLM to train a much smaller router LLM how to retrieve, using an LLM-as-a-judge based reward function.
From my own experience, these learned methods from Apple, Spotify and others, are highly relevant to hyperscale only - when you are dealing with hundreds of millions of items to choose from (or more), and require super high relevance in the top-5. For all other use cases (up to a few million items) I found that just building a BM25 index, and giving the LLM a BM25 "search tool" and casting a "wide net" wins every single time compared to learned methods (though the latter are more publishable in recsys and icml).
[1]
https://research.atspotify.com/2025/9/you-say-search-i-say-r...

comments.author: comandillos
comments.text: I feel like retrieval approaches, despite how good your ranking mechanisms are, end up biasing LLMs into what a heuristics-based system with way worse understanding of the domain says. I guess is a trade off between speed and quality, but letting the LLM explore without a bias (based on my personal experience) seems to generally provide much better results in terms of quality for the final output.

comments.author: mickeyp
comments.text:
I'm not sold; that's not to say I can't be swayed, but I've spent a lot of time building RAG solutions as a "one-size-fits-all" against codebases and I am not convinced embedding models or any of the myriad BERT implementations work well enough that they can beat out grep.
Most embedding/BERT models are far too small to truly grasp the nettles when an AI ask questions to them; and if you condition the AI to only search for really basic things, then... you're basically back to grep + regex.
You need to prune all manner of useless detritus that might gum up your matches like test files, documentation, and sidecars that semantically overlap or you're just going to match your tests. That's fine if you're building a document store for a business, but if you want a "one-and-done" solution for your codebase it's rarely good enough.
And if you
do
use a very large embedding model (which means it'll require running in the cloud as most company computers won't run it well), then... well, you're better off just using a language model as a subagent to scout ahead for you and elide the embedding model to begin with.

comments.author: jsw97
comments.text:
Maybe this is what the author is getting at, but if LP solvers are useful tools for editing weights, then Astra access to this methodology might make it more effective at weight editing.
The interpretation here is not so much that an LP can do Astra's work -- after all the Astra prompt was "improve Qwen's math by changing weights" or similar. Instead, it's that with some guidance (eliminate this behavior, preserve that behavior, as expressed through linear constraints) the solver is much more efficient than Astra's trial and error. So essentially the solver would be a way of cutting through all the time consuming stuff and expressing Astra's intent more immediately. And then presumably Astra could iterate on that to a better solution.
The use of an LP solver here is a really cool insight.
